governanceModel: New AI Basic Act layered on an AI economy widely described as chip-centric rather than model-centric

overview:
Taiwan's AI Basic Act passed the Legislative Yuan in December 2025 and took effect on 14 January 2026, adopting an EU-AI-Act-aligned definition of AI and seven core principles: sustainable development and wellbeing, human autonomy, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency, fairness, and accountability. The Act also requires the Executive Yuan to form a national AI strategy committee to draft Taiwan's first AI development blueprint, though its current operational status (fully constituted versus still forming) is not yet clearly confirmed.

Compared with most peer economies profiled here, Taiwan's AI story is often framed around chips rather than models — TSMC's role in the global AI hardware supply chain appears to receive far more policy and media attention than any domestic frontier AI software lab, and Taiwan does not currently appear to have a lab operating at a scale comparable to Japan's Sakana AI or France's Mistral. As of mid-2026, Taiwan is reportedly considering export-control rules on AI chips to China that go beyond the existing US blacklist, with potential implications for TSMC and its supply chain if adopted.

currentDirection.summary: Taiwan moved relatively quickly to pass a comprehensive AI Basic Act, and is reportedly considering going further than existing US chip-export rules on sales to China — a move that, if adopted, would represent a distinctly supply-chain-driven form of AI policy tightening given TSMC's role in global AI hardware.

recentDevelopments.text: A Keelung court detains three Super Micro and Albatron executives (~1 July 2026) in what is reported as Taiwan's first criminal probe into diversion of NVIDIA AI chips to China — a case widely read as exposing a legal gap, since Taiwan does not yet criminalise AI-chip exports to China even as US rules restrict them.
Taiwan's exports rise 40.3% year-on-year in June, reportedly driven largely by strong global demand for AI chips.

Taiwan is reported (Bloomberg, June 2026) to be weighing tighter AI-chip export controls on China to align with the US — potentially a criminal ban on exports above a compute-performance threshold to all Chinese buyers, going beyond the existing US blacklist — which could raise risks for TSMC and server makers like Foxconn if adopted; TSMC shares slipped on the reports.
Cabinet moves to form a national AI strategy committee to draft Taiwan's first AI development blueprint; whether the committee has been fully constituted as of mid-2026 is not yet clearly confirmed.
AI Basic Act enters effect, adopting an EU-AI-Act-aligned definition and seven core principles.

policyAndRegulation.title: AI Basic Act
policyAndRegulation.summary: Passed the Legislative Yuan 23 December 2025, in effect since 14 January 2026. Adopts an EU-AI-Act-aligned definition of AI and seven core principles covering sustainable development, human autonomy, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency, fairness and accountability.

policyAndRegulation.title: Taiwan AI Action Plan 2.0
policyAndRegulation.summary: Four-year national AI plan running 2023-2026, now in its final year.

policyAndRegulation.title: Proposed AI chip export controls on China
policyAndRegulation.summary: Reportedly under consideration as of mid-2026 — Bloomberg reported Taiwan weighing curbs to align with the US, potentially a criminal ban on exports above a compute-performance threshold to all Chinese buyers, going beyond the existing US blacklist. The July 2026 detention of Super Micro and Albatron executives over alleged NVIDIA-chip diversion highlighted that Taiwan does not yet criminalise such exports. If adopted, controls could carry implications for TSMC and server makers like Foxconn.

researchEcosystem.summary: Taiwan's AI ecosystem is often characterised as chip-centric rather than model-lab-centric: TSMC's role in global AI chip manufacturing receives substantially more attention than domestic AI software development, and Taiwan does not currently appear to have a frontier AI model lab operating at a scale comparable to some regional peers. The clearest domestic model effort is the government-backed TAIDE (Trustworthy AI Dialogue Engine), a Taiwan-focused traditional-Chinese large language model developed with the National Center for High-performance Computing (NCHC) under NARLabs and framed partly as a defence against Chinese-language AI influence; Taiwan is reported to have earmarked up to around NT$17.4B (~US$556M) through 2026 for related AI research. Universities such as National Taiwan University and applied bodies like the Institute for Information Industry (III) anchor much of the research and talent base.

debates.topic: AI chip export controls on China beyond the existing US blacklist
debates.summary: Taiwan is reportedly considering export restrictions on AI chips to China that go further than current US rules — a move that, if adopted, could have significant consequences for TSMC and its server-maker customers.
debates.expanded: Because TSMC manufactures a large share of the world's most advanced AI chips, any Taiwanese export-control decision could have outsized global impact compared with a similar decision by most other governments. Server makers like Foxconn could face supply-chain risk if restrictions tighten further, while some national-security-focused commentators argue Taiwan has an incentive to align closely with US controls given its own security relationship with Washington.

debates.topic: Building an AI ecosystem around chips rather than models
debates.summary: Taiwan's AI policy conversation appears to be shaped more by hardware and supply-chain questions than by model development or deployment risk, in contrast to many peer economies.
debates.expanded: Unlike most economies profiled here, Taiwan does not appear to have a domestic frontier AI software lab of comparable scale to build policy around — its AI Basic Act and the planned national AI strategy committee are intended to define what an AI development blueprint looks like for an economy whose comparative advantage lies in manufacturing chips that other countries' AI models run on, rather than in building the models themselves.

debates.topic: A sovereign Mandarin model against Chinese-language AI influence
debates.summary: The government-backed TAIDE model is framed less as a bid for the frontier than as a way to ensure a trusted, Taiwan-centric traditional-Chinese AI that reflects local language, values and security concerns rather than mainland Chinese ones.
debates.expanded: TAIDE (Trustworthy AI Dialogue Engine), developed with the National Center for High-performance Computing, was trained largely on Taiwanese-sourced data — including Central News Agency articles — and is presented partly as a safeguard against dependence on Chinese-origin Mandarin models that could carry different political framings or censorship. Supporters argue a sovereign Mandarin model matters for information security and cultural autonomy; sceptics note that TAIDE operates well below the scale of leading global models and question whether a state-led effort can keep pace, reinforcing the view that Taiwan's real AI leverage lies in hardware rather than models.

notableGaps.note: No Taiwan-based lab trains frontier-scale general-purpose models; the main domestic effort, the government-backed TAIDE, is a comparatively small sovereign traditional-Chinese model, consistent with an AI economy centred on chip manufacturing rather than model development.

Taiwan does not appear to have a standalone national AI safety institute of the kind emerging in Japan, South Korea and Singapore; AI-safety and governance work is spread across the National Science and Technology Council, the Ministry of Digital Affairs and bodies such as the Institute for Information Industry.
